newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian fund aims to trade $100 mln debt locally.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian fund aims to trade $100 mln debt locally.

text.p: A private-sector initiated mutual fund to list Nigeria's internationally quoted debt instruments locally aims to trade upto $100 million of the debt on the Lagos stock exchange, the promoters said on Tuesday.

"The total size of the fund is $100 million and it will be issued in a series of tranches beginning with $16 million," said Phillip Ihenacho of U.K.-based Afrinvest Securities Limited at a presentation of the fund in Lagos.
The fund, to be launched on February 17, will be invested in promissory notes and par bonds issued by Nigeria abroad and will run for three weeks.

"The minimum investment will be $5,000 but investors can get it at the secondary market in units of $1,000," said Godwin Obaseki, managing director Securities Transactions and Trust Company, the issuing house for the fund.
The promoters expect an actual yield of around eight percent after all expenses.
They said the fund, which will be the first listing on the Nigerian Stock Exchange of any international capital market instruments, had received all the necessary official approvals.
Nigerian promisory notes, issued abroad since 1988 in settlement of its trade debt, are worth $5 billion while its par bonds worth $2 billion have been traded abroad since 1992.
Ihenacho said it had been difficult for Nigerian investors to invest in the country's government bond.
"With the listing of this fund it will be possible for both local and international investors to invest through the Nigerian capital markets in these instruments," he said.
The fund was developed over the last year and involves Citibank's local subsidiary, the Nigeria International Bank (NIB) and the United Bank for Africa, one the country's top three banks.

"This is a new trend and will send a strong signal to the international investing community that Nigerians have confidence in our economy," said Obaseki, adding "it will also ensure that some of the payments made by the Nigerian government on its foreign obligations are brought home."
Nigeria owes a total of $28 billion abroad although 65 percent of it is to the Paris Club of government creditors which has remained unserviced for several years.
On the other hand, the oil-rich nation is known to regularly service its London Club debt to commercial banks.
"Nigeria has been very good at servicing its commercial debt and this fund will make Nigerians also benefit from these debt instruments," said a senior official of UBA.
